extracted.intended_audience: railway engineers, engineering policymakers, and engineering historians
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria for designing and operating railways, locomotives, and associated safety systems — emphasizing mechanical limits, routing/gradient choices, propulsion selection, and commercial viability. Drawn from George Stephenson's practical judgments and testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-acting carriage brakes (momentum-operated with guard control)
rubrics_metrics.description: His plan consisted in employing the momentum of the running train to throw his proposed brakes into action, immediately on the moving power of the engine being checked. He would also have these brakes under the control of the guard, by means of a connecting line running along the whole length of the train, by which they should at once be thrown out of gear when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the most important arrangement for increasing railway safety: would 'scarcely any accident could take place.' Accompanying benefits include reduced tear and wear of engines, carriages, tenders, and brake-vans. Stephenson urged legal enforcement if necessary. (Context: safety design should include automatic actuation plus human override/control.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic signals worked by locomotives
rubrics_metrics.description: He suggested that the signals of the line should be self-acting, and worked by the locomotives as they passed along the railway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offered as an additional means of safety alongside self-acting brakes — i.e., signalling should be automatic and integrated with train movement to reduce human error and improve overall safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit railway speeds for safety and economy
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I do not like either 40 or 50 miles an hour upon any line—I think it is an unnecessary speed; and if there is danger upon a railway, it is high velocity that creates it. I should say no railway ought to exceed 40 miles an hour on the most favourable gradient; but upon a curved line the speed ought not to exceed 24 or 25 miles an hour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher speeds increase strain on road and rolling stock, requiring heavier engines and better-fastened/heavier rails and immediately increasing working expenses. Speed choices must balance public need against material limits and lifecycle costs. Stephenson notes that while 50+ mph might be safe with 'perfect' materials, real-world iron fatigue and hidden flaws make lower speeds preferable for safety and economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design with realistic material strength limits (iron fatigue & hidden flaws)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There are limits to the strength of iron, whether it be manufactured into rails or locomotives; and there is a point at which both rails and tyres must break... iron, even the best, will "tire," and with constant use will become more and more liable to break at the weakest point—perhaps where there is a secret flaw that the eye cannot detect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and operational standards must account for material fatigue and manufacturing variability. Do not assume 'perfect iron'; allow safety margins in rail and vehicle design, and select construction/maintenance regimes that detect and mitigate hidden defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer flat gradients and avoid the 'undulating' system
rubrics_metrics.description: His practice ... was to secure a road as nearly as possible on a level, following the course of the valleys and the natural line of the country: preferring to go round a hill rather than to tunnel under it or carry his railway over it, and often making a considerable circuit to secure good, workable gradients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical experiments showed substantial losses of locomotive power on inclines (engine expends half its power on a rising gradient of 1 in 260; at 1 in 100 not less than three-fourths sacrificed). Long flat lines yield better paying qualities for hauling minerals, merchandise, and passengers — even if they cost more to construct initially. Route design should prioritize operational economy and haulage efficiency over minimal construction distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Route selection must prioritize operational economy over short-term construction savings
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The longer flat line must eventually prove superior to the shorter line of steep gradients as respected its paying qualities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware 'direct line' mania that favors shorter, cheaper-to-construct routes with worse gradients and sharper curves. Committees or promoters choosing the cheapest construction option risk imposing higher long-term operating costs and neutralizing locomotive improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose propulsion on grounds of commercial efficiency, reliability, and all-weather performance
rubrics_metrics.description: He stood by the locomotive engine; and subsequent experience proved that he was right. 'Nothing will beat the locomotive for efficiency in all weathers, for economy in drawing loads of average weight, and for power and speed as occasion may require.' The atmospheric system was 'ingenious' but 'costly, irregular in action, and, in particular kinds of weather, not to be depended upon.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate propulsion concepts by practical trials and by commercial criteria (cost, regularity, weather-dependence, maintenance). Ingenious theoretical mechanisms must prove profitable and dependable in service before wide adoption; stylistic or scientific novelty alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineers must ensure commercial viability and avoid speculative endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: They were not government roads, but private ventures ... they must be so laid out as not only to prove of decided public utility, but also to be worked economically and to the advantage of their proprietors. He repeatedly declared that if he did not believe they could be 'made to pay,' he would have nothing to do with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional responsibility includes assessing financial and traffic projections realistically and declining to support or endorse speculative schemes. Stephenson refused to lend his name to prospectuses and avoided speculative trading in shares; ethical practice may include reducing or deferring fees to help an undertaking succeed but not participating in unjustified promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough on-site surveying and evaluation of local resources and terrain
rubrics_metrics.description: He went carefully over the entire length of the proposed line ... examining the bearings of the coal-field, the slate and marble quarries, and the numerous iron-mines ... carefully exploring the ravines ... in order to satisfy himself that the best possible route had been selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feasibility assessments should include detailed inspections of geology, local industry and traffic generators, ravines, passes, and likely construction obstacles (e.g., tunnels). Use local resource and traffic appraisals to inform route choice, negotiate land and material concessions, and to determine whether estimated traffic justifies construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative and committee decisions should respect engineering evidence and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The result of the labours of Parliament was a tissue of legislative bungling ... Committees decided without judgment and without discrimination; it was a scramble for Bills ... The Board of Trade promulgated remarkable views respecting gradients ... which Mr. Stephenson considered would seriously curtail the utility and economy of railways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers and parliamentary committees should give weight to empirical engineering data and long-term operational considerations rather than transient speculative pressures or short-term construction savings. Engineering testimony (e.g., experiments on gradients) should be considered before granting powers or endorsing standards.
